name: Yu Ding
institution: H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology
abstract: The speaker published a book in 2019, entitled 'Data Science for Wind Energy,' in which a set of wind operational problems is framed through a general formulation of f(Y|X), where Y is the response on a turbine and X is the wind and environmental input. When Y is the wind power output, the conditional density, f(Y|X), is related to the power curve model of wind turbines and can be used to characterize a wind turbine's performance and production efficiency. When Y is the mechanical load, the conditional density, f(Y|X), is related to the load estimation and reliability management for the wind turbines. Modeling and understanding the dynamic in X itself is also important, because a good model of X leads to better wind forecasting. The book is therefore structured in three parts: wind field modeling for forecasting, power curve modeling for performance analysis, and turbine reliability and fault detection. In this talk, the speaker will discuss work related to the second part of the book and present examples in which data science solutions make sensible impact.

name: Juan Humberto Sossa Azuela
institution: Computing Research Center, National Polytechnic Institute (IPN), Mexico
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is the ability of machines to imitate intelligent human behaviors and develop human-like tasks. It combines algorithms that allow computers to: 1) Perceive their environment, 2) Learn from perceived data, 3) Solve problems, and 4) Make appropriate decisions, with the objective of carrying out functions that until now were only achievable by human beings. A Metaverse, on the other hand, is a shared digital world, where, as users, we can travel and interact through our own avatar in an immersive three-dimensional virtual world. Within a metaverse we can carry out a great variety of activities such as socializing, playing, working, shopping, remotely attending concerts or sporting events, etc. In this talk we will address some details about the horizontal technology of Artificial Intelligence, as well as about the metaverse and what role Artificial Intelligence plays in its establishment. Details will be given about the applications that are coming in the future and the necessary requirements for the establishment and acceptance of what in the near future will be the next digital leap of our humanity.

name: Dr. Kai Sonder
institution: CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center)
topic: Brave new world, use of AI in agricultural research
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming agriculture, from research to farm support. Within the CGIAR network, machine learning is applied to extrapolate soil, climate, and pest data with greater accuracy, improving soil maps, fertilizer recommendations, and climate adaptation strategies. Combined with advances in remote sensing and satellite imagery, AI enables near real-time insights on crop types, land-use change, and early detection of plant diseases, with hyperspectral data offering new opportunities to monitor traits and variety adoption. At CIMMYT, AI is also accelerating the analysis of the world's largest maize and wheat gene bank, helping identify traits like drought tolerance and disease resistance, and reducing the time and cost of breeding new resilient varieties. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) are being explored as cost-effective tools for agricultural extension, delivering site-specific advice to farmers, including those in remote areas. Yet, as adoption spreads, ethical challenges remain concerning energy use, environmental footprint, and data quality, which must be carefully addressed to ensure sustainable and responsible AI deployment.

name: Xiaoou Li
topic: Navigating the Data Gaps: Time Series Forecasting with Incomplete Information
abstract: Time series forecasting is a cornerstone of modern data-driven decision-making, from predicting stock prices to managing energy consumption. However, the integrity of these forecasts is critically challenged by a pervasive and often overlooked issue: missing data. This is particularly pronounced in real-world systems like smart buildings, where sensor failures, network outages, and other disruptions lead to incomplete time series. This talk will explore the fundamental problem of building resilient forecasting models that can handle these data gaps. While drawing from our recent work on robust electricity forecasting using a Concept Echo State Network (CESN), we will generalize the discussion to a broader framework applicable across various domains. We will present a novel approach that not only maintains high accuracy but also delivers meaningful insights, even when faced with imperfect information. This research aims to provide a path forward for advancing data-driven decision-making in a world where data is often incomplete.
